Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "The family photo catalogue began as a practical way to find pictures for birthdays and reunions, but it has gradually become a record of how the collection itself changed. My mother kept the first albums in a cedar cabinet in the front room. Each album had a handwritten year on its spine, although several of the dates were guesses made before anyone compared the photographs with letters or school records. When the cabinet was emptied in 2018, we found loose prints tucked behind the shelves, including a small envelope marked “summer, maybe 1964.” The envelope held pictures from two different trips, so we left the uncertain date in the notes rather than choosing one.

The catalogue now covers prints, negatives, slides, and digital files contributed by four branches of the family. It does not try to put every person into a single family tree. Instead, each entry records the people who can be identified, the place if it is known, and the source of the information. A photograph may have “Margaret and Helen, probably at the lake” in the description, with the word probably retained because no one has found a second image from that outing. Names are linked to separate records, so a later correction to a person’s spelling does not alter the original caption written on the back of a print.

1. Arrangement and description

The physical albums are numbered by their current shelf order, not by the years they cover. Album 1 contains photographs from about 1948 through 1956, while Album 2 begins with a group of undated studio portraits and continues into 1961. This arrangement preserves the albums as objects; it also means that a search for a year is more useful than a search for an album number. Each page has a catalogue reference in pencil on the reverse of its protective sleeve. The reference points to a digital record, but the sleeve can be removed without leaving marks on the photograph.

For each image, the catalogue includes a short title, a date or date range, a location when established, names with confidence notes, and a description of the physical item. We also record whether the image is a print, negative, slide, or scan, along with dimensions where those are useful. A note about the back of a print belongs in the same record as the image, including handwriting, studio stamps, and signs that a photograph was trimmed. We use “unknown” only when a field matters and has been checked; an empty location field does not mean that nobody tried to identify the place.

The identification notes distinguish direct evidence from family recollection. A name written on the back is entered as an inscription, not automatically treated as a confirmed identification. Aunt Celia once looked at a picture of a boy in a striped shirt and said, “That has to be Peter, because he always wore those.” Her memory helped us compare the boy’s age with school photographs, but the catalogue still lists him as possibly Peter. In another case, a postcard dated 1952 shows the same garden as an undated family snapshot, giving us a useful date range without establishing the exact day either picture was taken.

2. Scanning and files

We scan prints in color even when the original appears black and white, since the paper may have yellowed or faded unevenly. The unedited scan is kept as a preservation file, and a separate viewing copy can be cropped or adjusted for brightness. Those changes are noted when they affect how an image looks, but they do not replace the source scan. For negatives and slides, the catalogue records the frame number when it can be read. Some strips were cut years ago, and a few surviving pieces have no edge markings, so the frame information is not always available.

Digital files supplied by relatives are stored with the name they arrived under as well as a catalogue identifier. The supplied name can contain useful clues, but we do not assume that its date is right. One folder called “Grandpa’s 80th” contained pictures from at least three family gatherings, and its files had been copied from an older computer without their original dates. We preserved the folder name in the source notes and added separate descriptions for the images we could identify. The catalogue distinguishes a photograph of a printed photograph from a scan made directly from the original print.

The working index is shared among the relatives who help with identification, while high-resolution files remain in the family archive. A copy of the index is kept on an external drive at my cousin Daniel’s house, apart from the main computer. We update both copies after a review session and note the date of the latest version. This arrangement is modest, but it has already helped when a laptop failed during a move. The catalogue does not contain every image file itself; it points to storage locations and records who supplied each item.

3. Review notes

We usually review a group of photographs together rather than sending a long list of names for people to answer on their own. The person who brought an image explains where it came from, and others can add memories or disagree. When two accounts conflict, both are recorded with their sources. In a picture from a 1970 picnic, one cousin remembers the location as Willow Point, while another recalls a park near the old ferry landing. The family has not found a sign or dated newspaper image that settles the question, so the location field remains open and both recollections appear in the notes.

The catalogue is useful beyond finding a particular picture. It has helped us notice that our oldest surviving photographs are concentrated on one side of the family, partly because those relatives lived near a portrait studio and kept the prints in albums. We have fewer images from the years when several households moved between towns, and the gap is visible in the date distribution. That pattern describes the collection, not the amount of time people spent together. We avoid treating a missing photograph as evidence that an event did not happen.

The next review is planned for the winter gathering, when several relatives who remember the early albums will be there. We will bring prints that have not yet been identified, including a group of small snapshots found in a tin of sewing supplies. The tin also held a bus ticket and a folded note, both kept with the photographs but catalogued as separate objects. No one has yet matched the ticket to a trip in the family letters.
